svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Where passkeys change the picture, and where they do not
svg.desc: A comparison of what a password requires against what a passkey requires. With a password, a secret is sent to the site and can be phished, reused, or stolen from the site's own database. With a passkey, a private key stays on your device, only a signature is sent, and the credential is bound to the site's identity so it cannot be presented to a lookalike. A band below states what does not change: the vault holding the passkeys becomes more important, not less, and most accounts still have a password behind the passkey.
svg.text: Figure 3: What a Passkey Changes About Your Vault
Your password manager now stores two different kinds of thing, and they fail in different ways.
a shared secret, sent to whoever asks convincingly

g.text: What leaves your device
The secret itself, every time you sign in.
Can be phished
A convincing lookalike page receives it and
can replay it. Your manager may decline to
fill, and you can still type it in yourself.
Can be stolen from the site
The site holds something derived from it, and
a breach of the site puts that at risk.
Can be reused
Which is the one failure a password manager
already solves, and the reason you have one.

svg.text: a key pair, bound to one site, that never leaves

g.text: What leaves your device
A signature over a fresh challenge. Never the
private key, and never anything replayable.
Resists phishing structurally
The credential is bound to the real site's
identity. A lookalike domain cannot request it,
and you cannot hand it over by mistake.
Survives a breach of the site
The site holds only a public key, which is
worth nothing to whoever steals it.
This is a genuine improvement, not a rebrand.

svg.text: What does not change, and what most coverage omits

g.text: The vault matters more, not less.
It now holds credentials that cannot be reset by changing a password.
Most accounts keep a password behind the passkey.
If the recovery path is still a password and a code by message, that is the real strength.
Sync means copies.
A passkey synchronised across devices lives wherever your vault lives, with all of Figure 1 applying to it.

svg.text: Adopt passkeys where they are offered. Then check what happens when you tell that site you have lost your device,
because that path is the one an attacker will use, and Lesson 4.4 is about exactly this.
